data.title: Acitretin
data.summary: I Retinoids · Second-generation (mono-aromatic) retinoid; active metabolite of etretinate
data.body:
_Oral · I Retinoids_

**Class:** Second-generation (mono-aromatic) retinoid; active metabolite of etretinate

## Mechanism of action
- Binds nuclear RAR and RXR receptors and changes gene transcription
- Normalises epidermal proliferation and differentiation
- Anti-inflammatory: reduces neutrophil migration (hence its good effect in pustular psoriasis)
- Not immunosuppressive — useful in HIV-associated psoriasis and in transplant recipients

## Pharmacokinetics
- Bioavailability about 60%, better with food; 95% albumin bound; half-life about 50 h
- With alcohol it is re-esterified to etretinate, which is stored in fat and has a half-life of 80–160 days
- This is why contraception must continue for years after stopping

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Psoriasis: pustular (generalised and palmoplantar) and erythrodermic respond best to monotherapy
- Plaque psoriasis: modest alone; much better combined with phototherapy (Re-PUVA, Re-NB-UVB), which also lowers UV dose
- Disorders of keratinisation: ichthyoses (lamellar, epidermolytic), Darier disease, PRP, palmoplantar keratoderma
- Hypertrophic and palmoplantar lichen planus; hypertrophic lupus erythematosus
- Chemoprevention of squamous cell carcinoma in organ-transplant recipients

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 25–50 mg once daily with the main meal (start at 25 mg; avoid high starting doses)
- Lower doses (10–25 mg) are often enough when combined with phototherapy
- Children (keratinisation disorders): about 0.5–1 mg/kg/day, using the lowest dose that works
- Capsules 10, 25 mg; full response in psoriasis may take 3–6 months

## Adverse effects
- Mucocutaneous: cheilitis, xerosis, 'sticky' skin, peeling of palms and soles, retinoid dermatitis, paronychia, pyogenic granuloma
- Hair loss (telogen effluvium, dose-related) is commoner than with isotretinoin
- Raised triglycerides and cholesterol; raised transaminases (rarely toxic hepatitis)
- Bone: DISH-like hyperostosis, extraspinal calcification, premature epiphyseal closure in children on long courses
- Pseudotumor cerebri, night blindness, myalgia
- Teratogenic (long-lasting because of etretinate formation)

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy, and women who may become pregnant within 3 years of stopping
- Breastfeeding; severe liver or kidney disease; chronic alcohol use; marked hyperlipidaemia
- Concurrent methotrexate (risk of hepatitis) or tetracyclines (pseudotumor cerebri)

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol → conversion to etretinate (long-lasting teratogenicity)
- Methotrexate: severe hepatotoxicity — avoid
- Tetracyclines: pseudotumor cerebri
- Progestin-only pill becomes unreliable
- Vitamin A: additive toxicity; phenytoin displaced from protein binding

## Monitoring
- Pregnancy tests: before, monthly during treatment, and periodically for 3 years after stopping
- Lipids and LFTs at baseline, then every 1–2 weeks for the first 1–2 months, then every 3 months
- Children on long courses: watch growth; X-ray only if bone symptoms appear

## Pregnancy & lactation
Absolute contraindication (old FDA category X). Contraception from 1 month before, throughout, and for 3 years after stopping. No alcohol during treatment and for 2 months after. No blood donation for 3 years.

## Viva points
- Best indications are pustular and erythrodermic psoriasis; for plaques, combine with UV (Re-PUVA)
- Alcohol turns acitretin into etretinate — hence 3 years of contraception
- It is not immunosuppressive, so it is safe in HIV and in transplant recipients
- Never combine with methotrexate

## Note on sources
Some Indian and European texts give 2 years of contraception after acitretin; Wolverton (US label) gives 3 years, which we follow.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.22; Khopkar (Oral retinoids). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
